transcript.content: Hi, welcome in—thanks for coming today. Can you tell me what brought you in to see me?

Well, what finally pushed me to come in is that my eating has been all over the place lately. Like, some weeks I barely touch dinner at all. But then other nights, I just stand in the kitchen eating crackers and sweets after everyone’s gone to bed. It’s so quiet then, you know? I used to love baking at night when I was in college. I took a few culinary classes as electives before I dropped out, and the smell of fresh bread at 2 AM is just... it's really something else. My roommate hated it though, she said the smell woke her up. She was a nursing major, always stressed out about exams. I wonder what she's up to now, probably working in some big hospital somewhere... but yeah, my appetite is just really unpredictable right now.
Over the past couple of weeks, have you noticed your mood feeling consistently down, sad, or empty most of the day?

Well, yeah, I do go through stretches where... it's like the whole house just feels gray and heavy, you know? I'll just sit at the kitchen table feeling completely empty, even though nothing terrible has actually happened that day. The table is this oak one that I got at a yard sale years ago. It was such a steal, honestly, only twenty bucks. The guy selling it was moving to Florida to be closer to his grandkids. Florida seems too hot for me, though. I've never been, but I imagine it's just humid all the time, and humidity always makes my hair frizz up so badly. I tried this new conditioner last week that was supposed to help with frizz, but it smelled like fake coconuts and I just couldn't stand it. But anyway, yeah, I just sit there and feel so down and empty for no real reason.
Have you ever had a period of several days where you felt unusually energetic, elated, or needed much less sleep than normal, even if your mood at other times has been low?

Oh, yes. I definitely get periods like that. Sometimes I'll wake up and just feel so bright and totally unstoppable, like I have all the energy in the world and can do absolutely anything. I usually try to use that energy for my painting. I have a little studio set up in the spare room, which actually used to be my son's room before he moved out to Seattle. He works in tech out there now. I don't know how he handles all that rain, honestly. I always tell him he needs to be taking Vitamin D supplements because the lack of sun can just ruin your system. I actually read this really fascinating article about it while I was waiting at the dentist last month. Dr. Evans, he's great, always has this very soothing classical music playing in the waiting room... 

But wait, what was I saying? Right, the energy. So when I get in those unstoppable moods, the weird thing is I can also flip and get suddenly furious over practically nothing. Like, just completely enraged if my husband moves my paints even an inch from where I left them, or if he questions a receipt from the craft store. He always squints at my receipts like he's auditing me, even though he was a mechanic, not an accountant. He used to work on these gorgeous vintage cars. There was this one cherry red Chevy he fixed up years ago, I always wonder who ended up buying that car... but yeah, I do get those really energetic periods.
When you have one of these unusually energetic and 'unstoppable' periods, how many days in a row does it typically last?

Well, I'm not really sure how many days exactly. I don't usually keep track on a calendar or anything like that. Calendars always make me feel so boxed in, you know? My sister-in-law, she has this massive color-coded family planner on her fridge. Every little thing is scheduled—soccer practice, dentist appointments, when to buy groceries. She even schedules when she waters her plants. I could never live like that. I tried keeping a planner once, back when I was taking those culinary classes, but I just ended up drawing little doodles of pastries in the margins instead of writing down my assignments. I drew this one croissant that looked so realistic it actually made me hungry just looking at it. I've always loved French pastries. There's this little bakery downtown that makes the most incredible eclairs, but parking down there is just a total nightmare since they put in those new bike lanes... so yeah, I don't really know how many days it lasts.
During those energetic, unstoppable periods, do you find you need much less sleep than usual—like only a few hours—and still feel fine the next day?

Oh, definitely. It's like I don't even need it. I can sleep maybe three or four hours, and I'll wake up feeling completely charged up, just ready to go. I'll start writing blog posts or planning out all these new projects before the sun is even up. I actually started a blog a few years ago about restoring old furniture. I got the idea after I fixed up this beautiful mahogany dresser I found on the side of the road. Someone had just left it there! Can you believe that? People throw away the most amazing things. My neighbor, Mrs. Gable, she's always throwing out perfectly good gardening tools just because they have a little rust on them. I keep telling her a little vinegar and baking soda will take that right off. Vinegar is so useful, honestly. I use it for cleaning my windows, too. The commercial window cleaners always leave these awful streaks, and they smell so strongly of ammonia. Ammonia gives me such a headache. I had a headache for three days straight last month, and I swear it was from the cleaning lady at the grocery store mopping the floors... but yeah, I wake up feeling totally fine on just a few hours of sleep.

During those high-energy periods, have they ever caused serious problems—like trouble at work, conflicts with family, or even needing to go to the hospital—or have you always been able to function normally despite the reduced sleep and heightened energy?

Well, it definitely causes some problems, yes. I mean, I wouldn't say I end up in the hospital or anything like that, but it does make things difficult. Like with my facilitator training I was doing—I just completely fell behind on it. And my private blog work, too. I had all these ideas, but when I tried to actually sit down and organize my projects or explain things, it just got so jumbled up and hard to put together. It's frustrating because I usually love organizing things. I used to organize my grandmother's button collection when I was little. She had this huge tin, an old butter cookie tin, filled with thousands of buttons. Some of them were glass, some were pearl, some were shaped like little animals. There was this one tiny brass button shaped like an owl that I was just obsessed with. Owls are so fascinating, aren't they? They can turn their heads almost all the way around. I saw a documentary about owls on PBS the other night. They have this incredibly silent flight because of the way their feathers are structured. It's a marvel of evolution, really... 

But anyway, what was I saying? Oh, right, the problems. Yeah, so the blog and the training got all messy. And then there's the tension at home with my husband. When I get like that, it just makes it so much harder to keep up our normal routines. We end up bickering more, usually about silly things, but it throws off the whole day.
Between these low periods and the energetic, unstoppable periods, have there been times—lasting two months or more—where your mood felt completely normal and stable?

Well, two whole months? I don't know if it's ever been quite that long. But I’ve definitely had several weeks at a time where I wasn't especially high or low. My mood felt pretty normal, really. But even during those okay weeks, things weren't completely quiet... I still felt absolutely sure that people online were tracking my garden photos. 

I take a lot of pictures of my hydrangeas. Hydrangeas are so incredibly tricky, you know? You have to get the soil pH just exactly right if you want them to be blue instead of pink. I started adding coffee grounds to my flower beds last spring because I read in a magazine that it makes the soil more acidic. My favorite coffee shop on Elm Street actually gives away their used espresso grounds for free in these little silver bags. It's such a brilliant way to recycle. They have this amazing cold brew there, too, which I normally don't even like because cold coffee usually tastes so bitter to me, but theirs is just so smooth. I think they steep it for twenty-four hours or something. My husband bought me a cold brew pitcher for Christmas so I could make it at home, but the glass cracked in the dishwasher the very first time I washed it. They really don't make things like they used to. 

But anyway... what was I saying? Oh, right, the tracking. Yeah, I was sure people were tracking the garden photos. And even when my mood was perfectly fine for those weeks, I still heard brief remarks when I was completely alone in the house. Just little comments out of nowhere when no one else was there. So, my mood was stable for a few weeks at a time, but those other things were still happening.
During those weeks when your mood felt stable—not high or low—about how long did you continue to hear those voices or feel that people were tracking your photos?

Well, like I said, it was for those several weeks at a time. My mood would be completely fine, not high, not low, just... normal. But the whole time, for those entire few weeks, I was still absolutely sure about the tracking. The people online, watching my garden photos. And the voices, too—those brief remarks when I was alone. They just kept happening the whole time my mood was stable. 

It's strange because you'd think if you feel fine, everything else would be fine, right? But no. It’s like when I tried to fix the leaky faucet in the downstairs bathroom. I thought it was just a loose washer, so I took the whole thing apart. I watched this YouTube video by this guy who calls himself the "Plumbing Professor." He had this really thick Boston accent, which reminded me of my uncle Arthur. Uncle Arthur used to live in Southie, and he’d always bring us these amazing cannolis from the North End whenever he visited. The pastry shells were so crispy, and the ricotta filling was just perfect, not too sweet. I tried to make cannolis from scratch once, but getting the dough thin enough is nearly impossible without one of those pasta roller machines. I keep meaning to look for one at the thrift store, but the thrift store downtown has gotten so expensive lately. They wanted twenty dollars for a used toaster last week! Can you believe that? 

Anyway... yeah, so for those several weeks when my mood was totally stable, the voices and the tracking feeling were still there the entire time.

When I get like that, it just makes it so much harder to keep up our normal routines. We end up bickering more, usually about silly things, but it throws off the whole day.

inference.note: History now includes clear hypomanic/manic-like episodes (decreased need for sleep, increased energy, irritability, goal-directed activity) alongside depressive episodes with functional impairment, supporting a bipolar spectrum diagnosis rather than unspecified mood episode alone. Added F31.81 (bipolar II) given hypomanic-level impairment without hospitalization, and F34.0 (cyclothymia) as a differential given chronic fluctuating pattern; retained F31.9 pending clarification of episode duration/severity.

doctor.intent: Determine if there have been extended stretches of stable, normal mood between the depressive and energetic episodes, which helps distinguish cyclothymia from a bipolar disorder with distinct mood episodes
doctor.question: Between these low periods and the energetic, unstoppable periods, have there been times—lasting two months or more—where your mood felt completely normal and stable?

target_item.name: Additional Requirement 3
target_item.manifestation: I’ve had several weeks at a time when I wasn’t especially high or low, but I still felt sure people online were tracking my garden photos and I still heard brief remarks when I was alone.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about periods of normal, stable mood between episodes, which corresponds to the patient's experience of having weeks without mood symptoms but still experiencing delusions and hallucinations.

patient.answer:
Well, two whole months? I don't know if it's ever been quite that long. But I’ve definitely had several weeks at a time where I wasn't especially high or low. My mood felt pretty normal, really. But even during those okay weeks, things weren't completely quiet... I still felt absolutely sure that people online were tracking my garden photos. 

I take a lot of pictures of my hydrangeas. Hydrangeas are so incredibly tricky, you know? You have to get the soil pH just exactly right if you want them to be blue instead of pink. I started adding coffee grounds to my flower beds last spring because I read in a magazine that it makes the soil more acidic. My favorite coffee shop on Elm Street actually gives away their used espresso grounds for free in these little silver bags. It's such a brilliant way to recycle. They have this amazing cold brew there, too, which I normally don't even like because cold coffee usually tastes so bitter to me, but theirs is just so smooth. I think they steep it for twenty-four hours or something. My husband bought me a cold brew pitcher for Christmas so I could make it at home, but the glass cracked in the dishwasher the very first time I washed it. They really don't make things like they used to. 

But anyway... what was I saying? Oh, right, the tracking. Yeah, I was sure people were tracking the garden photos. And even when my mood was perfectly fine for those weeks, I still heard brief remarks when I was completely alone in the house. Just little comments out of nowhere when no one else was there. So, my mood was stable for a few weeks at a time, but those other things were still happening.

inference.note: Patient reports persistent psychotic-like symptoms (belief of being tracked, hearing comments when alone) even during weeks of stable/euthymic mood, not confined to mood episodes. This argues against cyclothymia (F34.0), which excludes psychotic features, and raises concern for schizoaffective disorder (F25.0) given psychosis outside mood episodes. Also raises possibility of bipolar disorder with psychotic features (F31.2) given manic episodes with significant functional impairment (falling behind on training/blog, marital conflict), suggesting full mania rather than hypomania alone.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the psychotic symptoms (feeling tracked, hearing voices) persist independently of mood episodes for a significant duration (key for distinguishing schizoaffective disorder from bipolar with psychotic features)
doctor.question: During those weeks when your mood felt stable—not high or low—about how long did you continue to hear those voices or feel that people were tracking your photos?

target_item.name: Additional Requirement 3
target_item.manifestation: I’ve had several weeks at a time when I wasn’t especially high or low, but I still felt sure people online were tracking my garden photos and I still heard brief remarks when I was alone.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the duration of psychotic symptoms (hearing voices, delusions about tracking) during periods of stable mood, which corresponds to the requirement of psychotic symptoms occurring for 2 or more weeks in the absence of a major mood episode.

patient.answer:
Well, like I said, it was for those several weeks at a time. My mood would be completely fine, not high, not low, just... normal. But the whole time, for those entire few weeks, I was still absolutely sure about the tracking. The people online, watching my garden photos. And the voices, too—those brief remarks when I was alone. They just kept happening the whole time my mood was stable. 

It's strange because you'd think if you feel fine, everything else would be fine, right? But no. It’s like when I tried to fix the leaky faucet in the downstairs bathroom. I thought it was just a loose washer, so I took the whole thing apart. I watched this YouTube video by this guy who calls himself the "Plumbing Professor." He had this really thick Boston accent, which reminded me of my uncle Arthur. Uncle Arthur used to live in Southie, and he’d always bring us these amazing cannolis from the North End whenever he visited. The pastry shells were so crispy, and the ricotta filling was just perfect, not too sweet. I tried to make cannolis from scratch once, but getting the dough thin enough is nearly impossible without one of those pasta roller machines. I keep meaning to look for one at the thrift store, but the thrift store downtown has gotten so expensive lately. They wanted twenty dollars for a used toaster last week! Can you believe that? 

Anyway... yeah, so for those several weeks when my mood was totally stable, the voices and the tracking feeling were still there the entire time.

inference.note: Psychotic symptoms (tracking, voices) persisted continuously through several weeks of stable, non-elevated and non-depressed mood, indicating psychosis independent of mood episodes. This is inconsistent with bipolar disorder (F31.9, F31.2), where psychotic features should be confined to mood episodes, and instead supports schizoaffective disorder criteria requiring psychotic symptoms present for a substantial period without prominent mood symptoms.

opening_question.question: Hi, welcome in—thanks for coming today. Can you tell me what brought you in to see me?
